title: Indexes
subtitle: Speed up queries with CREATE INDEX and EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Without an index, finding a row by email requires scanning every row in the table — O(n) time. With 1 million users, that's a full table scan for every login query.
whyItExists.solution: An index is a separate data structure (B-tree) that maps column values to row locations. Finding rows by an indexed column is O(log n) instead of O(n).
whyItExists.whenToUse: Columns frequently used in WHERE, JOIN ON, or ORDER BY. Foreign key columns. Columns with high cardinality (many distinct values — email, username, UUID). Columns searched by range (price BETWEEN).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Columns rarely queried. Small tables (< a few thousand rows) — a scan may be faster than index overhead. Very low cardinality columns (is_active with only true/false) — a scan may be equally fast. Write-heavy tables where index maintenance cost outweighs read benefit.

explainModes.beginner: An index is like a book's index. Without it, finding 'chapter about JOINs' means reading every page. With the index, you jump directly to page 47. The database builds this lookup structure for you — you just tell it which column to index.
explainModes.simple: CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table(col). CREATE UNIQUE INDEX prevents duplicate values. DROP INDEX idx_name. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT ... shows whether the optimizer uses your index. A 'SCAN' means full table scan (no index). A 'SEARCH ... USING INDEX' means index is being used. Composite index: CREATE INDEX idx_name ON orders(user_id, ordered_at).
explainModes.standard: Primary key automatically has an index. UNIQUE constraint creates an automatic unique index. Index overhead: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update the index — indexes slow down writes. SQLite uses B-tree indexes. Index is most useful when query touches < ~10-20% of rows. Partial index: CREATE INDEX idx ON orders(total) WHERE status='pending' — only indexes rows matching the condition, smaller and faster.
explainModes.technical: Covering index: if all columns in a query are in the index, the database reads only the index (never touches the table) — very fast. Include columns with INCLUDE clause (PostgreSQL). SQLite automatically uses the best index using the query planner. ANALYZE updates table statistics, helping the planner make better decisions. REINDEX rebuilds an index (after corruption or major changes).
explainModes.deepDive: B-tree index: balanced tree where each node holds sorted key values and pointers. O(log n) for lookup, insert, delete. Range queries are efficient — the tree is sorted. Hash indexes (PostgreSQL) are O(1) for equality but don't support range queries. GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) for full-text search and JSONB. GiST for geometric types and full-text. BRIN (Block Range Index) for very large tables with correlated data (timestamps). Index bloat: after many updates/deletes, index pages have dead entries — VACUUM ANALYZE in PostgreSQL reclaims space.

content.code:
-- Show the query plan: does it use an index?
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'alice@example.com';
-- Result with index: SEARCH users USING INDEX idx_users_email
-- Result without: SCAN users

-- Check a JOIN plan
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT u.name, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.total > 1000;
-- Should show SEARCH orders USING INDEX and SEARCH users USING INDEX

-- Check sort plan
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY user_id, ordered_at;
-- With composite index: SCAN orders USING INDEX idx_orders_user_date
-- Without: SCAN + USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY

questions.question: Why do indexes slow down INSERT and UPDATE operations?
options: They don't — indexes only affect SELECT queries
The index data structure must be updated for every write, adding overhead
Indexes lock the table during writes
Indexes are rebuilt from scratch on every write
questions.explanation: Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE must also update every index on the affected columns. Adding a row to the table means inserting into the B-tree index too. For write-heavy tables, too many indexes slow down writes more than they help reads — so choose indexes deliberately based on actual query patterns.

faq.q: How do I know which indexes to create?
faq.a: Start with: (1) foreign key columns — always index them for JOIN performance, (2) columns in WHERE clauses of frequent, slow queries — use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to identify full table scans, (3) columns in ORDER BY for pagination queries. Don't pre-create indexes speculatively — measure first, index second.

examples: CREATE INDEX idx_posts_author ON posts(author_id) — fast posts-by-author query
CREATE INDEX idx_events_ts ON events(occurred_at) — fast time-range queries
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN before deploying a new query in production
